entries.title: Englewood dad fatally shot in his home was family's 'protector,' fiancé says
entries.summary: <p>Jennifer Lacey felt like 2026 was going to be her year. </p><p>She had just gotten promoted at work. Her kids were doing well. And she had just moved into a new home with her fiancé, Antwan Washington.</p><p>Then her 11-year-old son woke up to find bullet holes in the living room wall and his dad motionless on the couch. At first, Lacey thought he was asleep.</p><p>"From the position he was sitting, it looked like he was asleep," Lacey said. "So I tapped him, like, 'Babe, get up. You have to get to work.' ... He just falls to the right, and that's when I see that he was shot in the head. ... Just the worst day of my life, ever."</p><p>Washington, 45, had been shot in the head and was pronounced dead on the scene, according to Chicago police.</p><p>He was in his home watching TV in the 5700 block of South May Street around 5 a.m. Saturday when two people got out of a gray 4-door sedan and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/28/man-fatally-shot-inside-englewood-home" >fired handguns into the apartment</a>, according to a police report. The car fled the scene. Police found 16 shell casings in the intersection.</p><p>"He wasn't doing anything but doing his normal morning routine: getting up in the morning, you know, washing up, brushing his teeth, you know, getting dressed and making his coffee and smoking his cigarette," Lacey, 33, said through tears.</p><p>The police report states that someone else in the building was the intended target of the shooting.</p><p>"There's really no motivation for it," Lacey said. "We're just a working family just wanting to raise our kids." </p><p>Now Lacey is grappling with the aftermath of his death. She must now raise their four sons without their father. Her future plans are shattered: a housewarming party at their new home, hosting family for barbecues and watching their kids grow up. Washington also leaves behind a 21-year-old son from a previous relationship, she said.</p><p>"I will continue to let my kids know how much he did love them, how much of a leader he was, and how much positivity he instilled in them as children," she said.</p><p>Lacey described Washington as a "protector" who worked hard and loved his family. He could often be found playing video games with his sons, barbecuing in the summer and listening to Earth, Wind & Fire or 2Pac. He was a manager at an Englewood Chipotle and had recently moved to manage a team at a Bridgeport location, Lacey said.</p><p>No one is in custody, police said.</p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://www.gofundme.com/f/support-for-antwans-family-after-tragic-loss" target="_blank" >GoFundMe</a> set up by his fiancée had raised $2,500 of a $10,000 goal by Monday night. It said the "simple moments meant everything to him and his family."</p><p><i>Contributing: Violet Miller</i></p>

entries.title: Miguel Vargas’ grand slam helps White Sox shake off season-opening ‘jitters’ for first win
entries.summary: <p>MIAMI — Maybe they just needed a few extra days to warm up.</p><p>After only showing signs of life late in a disastrous opening weekend, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> hitters found their stride Monday against the Marlins, clubbing their way to a 9-4 victory for their first triumph of the season.</p><p>A monster six-RBI night from Miguel Vargas in humid Miami made the Sox’ season-opening misery in blustery Milwaukee feel hundreds of miles away, even if their pitching woes kept things more interesting than fans would like.</p><p>Everson Pereira warmed up the Sox in the third inning by lining a double down the left-field line. He later scored on a single by Vargas.</p><p>Munetaka Murakami didn’t extend his historic three-game home-run streak to start his MLB career, but he did notch his first hit to stay in the park on a dribbler down the third-base line that set the stage for a three-run homer by Austin Hays, his first blast since <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/03/21/white-sox-outfielder-austin-hays-brings-steadying-force-to-lineup" target="_blank" ><u>signing with the Sox</u></a>.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Stay fair. IT WILL ❗️ <a href="https://t.co/cMZwl8mN2D">pic.twitter.com/cMZwl8mN2D</a></p>— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) <a href="https://twitter.com/whitesox/status/2038760220638224720?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">March 30, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>In the fourth, Marlins starter Chris Paddack hit Luisangel Acuna with a pitch to load the bases after singles by Tristan Peters and Pereira. Then Vargas, a native of Cuba who lives in Miami, launched one 402 feet into the left-field seats for the Sox’ <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/03/29/white-sox-colson-montgomery-grand-slam-murakami-homer" target="_blank" ><u>second grand slam in as many days</u></a>. He had dozens of supporters in attendance at loanDepot Park.</p><p>‘‘Especially to have my family here and a couple of friends that never watched me play in the big leagues, it’s super-fun, and I’m very proud to accomplish what we accomplished today,’’ Vargas said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">MIGUEL VARGAS GRAND SLAM<br><br>LET’S GOOOOOO <a href="https://t.co/gmGOmxMhG5">pic.twitter.com/gmGOmxMhG5</a></p>— Mike (@ChiSoxFanMike) <a href="https://twitter.com/ChiSoxFanMike/status/2038764128932676030?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">March 30, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>But no lead feels particularly comfortable for Sox pitchers, and right-hander Davis Martin served up a two-run homer to Liam Hicks in the fourth. The Marlins struck again in the fifth with an RBI single by Jakob Marsee.</p><p>All told, Martin allowed three runs and five hits with six strikeouts and two walks in five innings.</p><p></p><p>The Sox added a run in the sixth when Acuna walked, stole second and third and then slid home on a shallow sacrifice fly by Vargas, his sixth RBI of the evening.</p><p></p><p>Offseason addition Sean Newcomb was strong in relief until a triple by Marsee and a single by Otto Lopez narrowed the Sox’ lead to 9-4 in the eighth. He left a bases-loaded jam for Jordan Hicks to shut down.</p><p></p><p>After thwacking a grand slam in a losing cause when the Sox’ bullpen melted down Sunday against the Brewers, Colson Montgomery said he and other Sox hitters finally were shaking off <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/03/28/colson-montgomery-white-sox-year-2" target="_blank" ><u>some early-season nerves</u></a>. After being outscored 20-3 in their first two games, the Sox have stacked up 16 runs in two days.</p><p></p><p>‘‘We all progressively just kept getting better,’’ said Montgomery, who needed 74 career games to sock his first two grand slams, the fastest in Sox history. ‘‘We are seeing the ball a lot better, having better-quality at-bats. I think it was the jitters and we were all really excited.’’</p><p></p><p>Pereira acknowledged as much before his second consecutive multihit game after flailing through three strikeouts on Opening Day.</p><p></p><p>‘‘I’m one of those players that is really excited, and I want to crush every single pitch,’’ Pereira said. ‘‘Just try to slow the game down and breathe.’’</p><p></p><p>Now the Sox are hoping the offensive results multiply.</p><p></p><p>‘‘It’s just part of the game,’’ manager Will Venable said. ‘‘You spend all this time in spring training and going about your business, and then the lights come on and it means something and it changes a little bit. You’ve just got to find your bearings again.’’</p><p></p><p>Vargas found his bearings while borrowing Murakami’s first-baseman’s mitt.</p><p></p><p>‘‘He got three homers in three games, and now I use it and I got one,’’ Vargas said. ‘‘So I might be keeping it with me.’’</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.summary: <p>MIAMI — The first several games of the automated ball/strike era have been a mixed bag for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a>.</p><p>Catcher <b>Edgar Quero</b> hasn’t been shy about questioning umpires under the new ABS challenge system implemented <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-media/2026/02/12/how-abs-challenge-system-will-affect-mlb-tv-broadcasts-chicago-cubs-white-sox-spring-training-schedules" target="_blank" ><u>this season</u></a>, but Sox hitters still are feeling it out.</p><p>‘‘We’ve seen them less willing to pull the trigger on some challenges,’’ manager <b>Will Venable</b> said. ‘‘And I don’t get instant feedback on all these pitches on where they’re at, but it seems like we’re seeing less challenges from hitters.’’</p><p>Through four games, <b>Lenyn Sosa</b>, <b>Tristan Peters</b> and <b>Munetaka Murakami</b> are the only Sox batters to challenge calls. Sosa and Peters were wrong, but Murakami wiped out a miscalled strike Monday.</p><p>Quero has challenged nine calls behind the plate, getting four bad ones overturned. Sox pitchers have yet to initiate a review.</p><p>So should the Sox be quicker to tap their hat or helmet?</p><p>‘‘If they’re right, yeah,’’ Venable said with a laugh. ‘‘We want to make sure we’re challenging the right pitches. . . . It’s still new for a lot of these guys.’’</p><p>Venable didn’t tip the Sox’ ABS playbook, but he said ‘‘a mid-at-bat challenge is different than a potential strikeout or walk at-bat-ending challenge. There’s different things, different parts of the zone that we’ve talked about, different guidelines.’’</p><p>Quero said he’ll keep going with his gut.</p><p>‘‘Yeah, [based on] good feelings and . . . seeing the ball, where it’s coming from, and knowing the strike zone a little bit better,’’ he said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure in Milwaukee was his first big-league action in 2½ years. He joined the Sox on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/02/19/white-sox-anthony-kay-looks-to-carry-over-success-from-japan" target="_blank" ><u>a two-year, $12 million contract</u></a> during the offseason after rejuvenating his career with a stint in Japan.</p><p>‘‘I’ve just grown so much mentally those couple of years in Japan,’’ Kay, 31, said. ‘‘That’s been a huge difference for me in my career.’’</p><p>It wasn’t pretty, but Kay turned in the best start of the Sox’ abysmal opening series, giving up two runs and three hits, striking out five and walking four in 4⅔ innings.</p><p>‘‘Definitely got a little emotional walking out to the bullpen before the game,’’ Kay said. ‘‘Definitely was a little amped up and had to hone that in a little bit. I think I did a good job of settling in after that.’’</p><p>It wasn’t exactly the season-opening sensation the Sox have gotten from a certain other Japanese veteran on their roster, but they are relying on Kay to eat up some serious innings this season while waiting for a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/02/12/noah-schultz-hagen-smith-white-sox-spring-training-triple-a" target="_blank" ><u>a wave of talented arms</u></a> to emerge from Triple-A Charlotte.</p><p>Kay got a preview of new teammate <b>Munetaka Murakami’s</b> prodigious power while facing him overseas.</p><p>‘‘I’m not surprised by it,’’ Kay said of Murakami’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/03/29/white-sox-colson-montgomery-grand-slam-murakami-homer" target="_blank" ><u>three home runs</u></a> in his first three MLB games. ‘‘I know some people are, but I’ve seen it.’’</p><h3>Numbers game</h3><p>Before Opening Day, Quero switched his jersey number from the 7 he debuted with last season to 26, which he said holds personal significance as a combination of the birthdates of his mother, his sister and his own.</p><p>It’s also the number catcher <b>Korey Lee</b> wore for the Sox until being designated for assignment at the end of spring training, ending up as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/03/22/white-sox-sign-catcher-reese-mcguire-leaving-korey-lee-as-odd-man-out" target="_blank" ><u>the odd man out</u></a> when general manager <b>Chris Getz</b> signed superior pitch-framer <b>Reese McGuire</b>.</p><p>Lee cleared waivers and now is wearing No. 26 at Charlotte.</p><div class="PageListL" entries.title: Michael Busch has grown into indispensable member of Cubs' lineup
entries.summary: <p>In Michael Busch’s first at-bat Monday night against the Angels at Wrigley Field, he walked on four pitches that didn’t come close to the strike zone.</p><p>After a breakout 2025 season that saw Busch finish third among first basemen in homers (34), seventh in RBI (90) and second in wRC+ (140), he has earned that respect from pitchers because they know he capitalizes on mistakes. So far this season, Busch has maintained his productive ways at the plate.</p><p>Busch isn’t the showman Pete Crow-Armstrong is, nor is he the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ clubhouse leader like Dansby Swanson or the All-Star like Alex Bregman. He’s an unassuming player who lets his game speak for itself — and it’s loud.</p><p>“He was the best first baseman in baseball last year,” Crow-Armstrong told the Sun-Times before the Cubs’ 7-2 victory. “I know you still got [Dodgers first baseman Freddie Freeman] and [Orioles slugger Pete Alonso]. But last year, I don’t think there was a better first baseman in baseball.”</p><p>Busch fits in with the measured and workmanlike group that team president of baseball operations Jed Hoyer has assembled. The Cubs traded left-handed pitching prospect Jackson Ferris and outfield prospect Zyhir Hope to the Dodgers for reliever Yence Almonte and Busch before the 2024 season.</p><p>At the time of the trade, Busch was the Dodgers’ No. 2 prospect, according to MLB.com, but was blocked from regular playing time because of their star-studded cast of future Hall of Famers at first and second base, and the designated hitter spot.</p><p>With regular playing time, Busch has flourished in Chicago. And now, after manager Craig Counsell said he’s going to use him more against left-handers, he’ll have even more responsibility, and Busch should fare well. He already sets the tone for the team as the leadoff hitter, even though he doesn’t fit the prototypical model of one. Crow-Armstrong said jokingly that Busch is “lacking a little bit of speed.”</p><p>“I love him in the leadoff spot,” Crow-Armstrong said. “His ability to get on base, and especially when he’s hot, makes things feel like an event.”</p><p>He’s a selective hitter with plus power and rarely chases. Crow-Armstrong lauded Busch for his work in the batting cages, saying that the first baseman works at a “very controlled level,” and that when the tempo speeds up in the game, he’s prepared for it.</p><p>“[Busch] knows what he can handle, and he does a really good job of swinging at the pitches that are right for him,” left fielder Ian Happ told the Sun-Times. “It’s not as easy as it sounds to do that. On Opening Day [Busch reached base four times and was 3-for-4 with two doubles] his ability to control the zone and get the pitches that he wanted to hit was impressive.”</p><p>Busch has room for improvement on defense. He graded out in the 36th percentile in outs above average.</p><p>“Think just being a little more efficient in all areas,” Busch said. “Especially [with] my footwork over at first, which is one thing that I want to take pride in, making sure I’m really comfortable with how I’m getting to the base, working around the base.”</p><p>But if Busch’s 2025 performance is his floor, the Cubs are in a good spot. He doesn’t garner the recognition of his teammates, but they understand Busch’s importance to the lineup.</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 entries.title: Onetime Spurs guard Tre Jones talks 'Iceman' nickname and Caleb Williams
entries.summary: <p>SAN ANTONIO – Tre Jones spent five-plus seasons wearing Spurs black and silver, learning the history of the organization.</p><p>The Bulls guard has also spent the last few years in Chicago, and doing so as a football fan of the Bears and quarterback Caleb Williams.</p><p>Those two worlds collided as Jones found himself stuck going between historian and politician.</p><p>There’s been a lot made of the “Iceman” nickname the last week, especially since in San Antonio there was only one “Iceman:” NBA legend George Gervin.</p><p>Williams tried to hijack the nickname and claim the legal copyright, which didn’t sit well in many circles, including with Gervin.</p><p>Jones has two horses in the race so was guarded on how he approached the entire saga.</p><p>“Yeah, the ‘Iceman,’ “ Jones said when Gervin’s name was mentioned. “George Gervin was a pioneer for basketball. Obviously, not only for (the Spurs) franchise, but the entire NBA as well. He pushed the envelope in so many ways.</p><p>“I think that as long as ‘The Iceman’ nickname isn’t disrespected and it’s kept as a sign of respect to George Gervin … you know it’s a new eras, a new generation, names can keep flying around like that.”</p><p>Plus, Jones and his Bulls teammates had a bigger nickname to worry about on Monday: “Wemby.”</p><p>Looking to avoid a winless four-game road trip, the Bulls watched current Spurs legend Victor Wembanyama put on a clinic on both ends of the floor, scoring 41 points, grabbing 16 rebounds and adding three blocks to his box score, as the home team ran away with it, 129-114.</p><p>Not that it hurt the big picture for Billy Donovan’s crew, as they dropped a half-game behind idle Milwaukee in the standings, but kept the No. 9 spot in the draft lottery odds.</p><p>And frankly after the first quarter, they were never really a threat to challenge the home team. The Bulls played San Antonio even in the first quarter 29-28, but Wembanyama and second-year guard Stephon Castle took over, combining for 23 points in the second quarter.</p><p>Not a good way to end a day that started with the news that Jaden Ivey was let go for behavior detrimental to the team.</p><p>“He’s a very talented player,” guard Josh Giddey said of the Ivey news. “Obviously the whole thing is kind of unfortunate in a way. I hope he gets the help he needs, whatever he’s going through or not going through. I do really hope he gets help. It’s not going to be with the Bulls anymore, but wherever it is I hope he gets it.”</p><p>Meanwhile, as far as the “Iceman” debate, Williams has been courtside for several Bulls games since being drafted by the Bears two years ago, and that hasn’t gone unnoticed by Bulls players. That’s why as much as Jones respects the tradition and history of San Antonio, he admittedly offered up support in what the quarterback was attempting to do.</p><p>“I like Caleb a lot,” Jones said. “He had a great year this year and the ‘Iceman’ nickname was really cool. I support that as well, but as long as there’s the respect that George Gervin deserves with it.”</p><p></p><p></p><h3>More on Jones</h3><p></p><p>Gervin wasn’t the only topic Jones had to address before the game.</p><p></p><p>Like his older brother, <b>Tyus</b>, Jones played at Duke, still bleeds blue and was horrified to watch his alma mater become the first No. 1 seed in the NCAA Tournament to lose after leading by at least 15 points at the half.</p><p></p><p>‘‘That was a tough one for sure,’’ Jones said of the game Sunday. ‘‘Last year was tough, missing free throws and the turnover at the end of the game. But this year, up 19 . . . I was back at the hotel with my family, and it was definitely tough.</p><p></p><p>‘‘I always back them. I think this is setting them up for something down the line, for sure. [Coach <b>Jon</b>] <b>Scheyer </b>has been to three straight Elite Eights now. Final Four last year. Moments away from a Final Four this year. So I think whatever is happening is just preparing them for the future, for sure.’’</p><p></p><h3>Fixer-upper</h3><p></p><p>Bulls coach <b>Billy Donovan </b>has seen a lot of positives from forward <b>Leonard Miller</b>.</p><p></p><p>The high-energy Miller joined the Bulls from the Timberwolves in the <b>Ayo Dosunmu</b> trade and has worked his way into the rotation and even some starts.</p><p></p><p>Donovan, however, wants to see him take the next step in his game.</p><p></p><p>‘‘It’s just, like, the detail of who’s he guarding? What coverage is he in? Who is in the action with him? When is he switching?’’ Donovan said. ‘‘Those are things that are happening fast where he can get caught there several times.
